title: Bundle Project Structure, Shared Python Code and Dependency Failures

concepts.heading: One Entry File, Many Files, and What Gets Synced
concepts.body: A bundle has exactly one entry file, `databricks.yml`. At professional depth the trap is mixing up three similarly named mappings. The top-level `include` lists additional bundle configuration files, such as `resources/*.yml`; a file that no glob matches is never parsed, so validation passes and its job or pipeline silently never deploys. `sync.include` and `sync.exclude` filter which files are uploaded, and `sync.paths` adds folders that sit outside the bundle root. Deployment uploads the files under the root, so a shared package in `libs/common_transforms/` beside the bundle folder never reaches the workspace unless the folder is added to `sync.paths` (together with the bundle root itself). Symptom: `ModuleNotFoundError` after a successful deploy. A large estate also needs repetition. A For each task repeats work at run time inside one job, with one schedule and one set of alerts. Python support for bundles creates one real job resource per table at deploy time from a metadata file, each with its own schedule, owner permissions and alerts.

concepts.heading: Building Wheels and Keeping Versions Fresh
concepts.body: Bundles can build a Python wheel through an `artifacts` mapping with `type: whl` and a build command, then attach it to job tasks. On serverless compute the environment of a task is cached, and Python identifies a wheel by name and version. A rebuilt wheel that still says `0.1.0` looks identical to the installed one, so the job keeps running old code. The serverless documentation states that changing a custom package requires updating its version number. For the bundle workflow, setting `dynamic_version: true` on the wheel artifact patches the version from the timestamp of the built file, so CI can redeploy without anyone editing `pyproject.toml`. Where the wheel is stored matters too. The DBFS root is writable by any workspace user, so storing libraries there is deprecated and disabled by default on current runtimes. Workspace files, Unity Catalog volumes or a package repository are the recommended homes. A volume is governed by privileges, so only a release service principal needs write access while jobs only read.

concepts.heading: Pipelines Resolve Dependencies Differently from Jobs
concepts.body: A job task can install the project through an environment or a libraries entry. A Lakeflow Pipelines pipeline does not behave the same way: its dependencies are declared in the pipeline's `environment` section, for example a pinned package or an editable install of the bundle's file path. Adding a library only to `pyproject.toml` leaves a pipeline failing with `ModuleNotFoundError` after redeploy. Pipelines support only SQL and Python. A JVM library cannot be added by an init script without unpredictable behavior, so run the JVM step as its own task on suitable compute that writes a Unity Catalog table, and let a later pipeline task read it. Serverless pipelines do not support init scripts at all. Even on classic compute, Databricks recommends the Environment settings, because external dependencies and init scripts raise the risk of breakage when the runtime upgrades. Declare pinned wheels, for instance from a `/Volumes/...` path, and test the pipeline automatically.

concepts.heading: Why Serverless Installs Fail
concepts.body: Serverless installs fail for a few repeatable reasons. First, Spark is part of the managed environment: installing PySpark, or any package that depends on it, stops the session before code runs. Package authors should list PySpark as a development dependency instead of a hard runtime requirement. Second, serverless does not pin a CPU architecture. A task can land on `aarch64` or `x86_64`, and the choice can change between runs. A wheel with native extensions is built for one architecture, so installs fail intermittently with unchanged code. Prefer pure-Python wheels, or ship both variants each constrained with a `platform_machine` marker. Third, dependencies are resolved before notebook code runs, and serverless has no compute-scoped environment variables, so setting `PIP_INDEX_URL` in a cell changes nothing. For a private mirror put `index-url` or `extra-index-url` in the dependency specification, or ask an admin to configure default package repositories. Diagnose by asking whether the failure happens before any user code runs.

examPoints: A question about modules missing after a successful deploy is testing `sync.paths` for folders outside the bundle root, or `include` for configuration files that were never parsed.

A job that keeps running old code from a rebuilt wheel is testing the unchanged version number and `dynamic_version`; a pipeline that cannot find a library is testing the pipeline `environment` section.

Intermittent install errors with native wheels point to architecture variants, a session that dies at setup points to PySpark in the dependency tree, and a private mirror needs `index-url` in the specification, not an environment variable in a cell.

quiz.q: A bundle's job imports a package from `libs/common_transforms/`, a sibling of the bundle folder. After `bundle deploy` the job fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`. Which change fixes it?
choices: Add the folder to the top-level `include` mapping so the CLI reads its configuration
Add `../../libs` and `.` to `sync.paths` so the folder is uploaded
Add the folder to `sync.exclude` so the CLI stops filtering the files from the upload
Copy the package into the DBFS root and set a cluster environment variable that points at it for every task
quiz.explain: `sync.paths` lets the sync include folders outside the bundle root. The top-level `include` only references bundle configuration files, `sync.exclude` removes files from the upload, and the DBFS root is a deprecated, overwritable library location.

quiz.q: A team rebuilds an internal wheel and redeploys; the serverless job keeps running the old behavior because the version in `pyproject.toml` never changes. What is the best fix?
choices: Set `dynamic_version: true` on the wheel artifact to patch its version
Switch the job to a classic cluster policy, because serverless never installs wheels from volumes
Set `PIP_INDEX_URL` in the first notebook cell so the task fetches the newest wheel at start
Install PySpark into the task environment so the wheel is rebuilt whenever the job session starts up
quiz.explain: The cached serverless environment treats the same name and version as already installed, so a new timestamped version forces a fresh install. The other options misdescribe volumes, run too late to affect dependency resolution, or break the session.

recap: Know which bundle mapping does what (`include` for configuration, `sync.paths` for code), keep wheel versions moving, declare pipeline libraries in `environment`, and read serverless install errors as PySpark, architecture or index problems.

title: UDFs: Pandas, Python, SQL and Unity Catalog Functions

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Built-ins and UDFs
concepts.body: Built-in Spark functions run inside the engine and are optimized for distributed processing. A Python UDF moves data between the JVM and a Python process, which is expensive at scale. The documentation recommends UDFs for ad hoc queries, manual data cleaning, exploratory work and small to medium datasets, and recommends built-in methods for large datasets and for anything that runs regularly or continuously, such as ETL and streaming. The professional decision therefore starts with a question: can a built-in express this? A regular expression extraction on three billion rows every hour belongs to `regexp_extract`, not to a Python UDF whose time shows up as serialization in the Spark UI. Use a UDF when logic is hard to express with built-ins, for example encryption, hashing, JSON parsing or validation. When a UDF is justified, pick the vectorized form: pandas UDFs transfer data with Apache Arrow and work on batches, which the documentation describes as vastly faster than row-by-row Python UDFs.

concepts.heading: Pandas UDF Flavors and Expensive Initialization
concepts.body: A pandas UDF receives pandas objects per Arrow batch. A Series to Series UDF is called once per batch, so anything initialized in its body repeats for every batch. When a function needs a large object such as a 600 MB model loaded from a volume, executors can spend most of their time deserializing it. The Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series variant takes an iterator of batches and yields output batches, so the model can be loaded once before the loop and reused for every batch in that task. The length of the whole output must equal the length of the whole input. Wrap the loop in `try/finally` when a resource has to be released. Related forms such as `mapInPandas`, `mapInArrow` and `applyInPandas` apply a function to whole DataFrames or groups rather than to a single column. The exam question is usually the symptom: repeated loading cost means move the initialization out of the per-batch call.

concepts.heading: Unity Catalog Functions: Privileges, Compute and Isolation
concepts.body: A Unity Catalog function is a governed object named `catalog.schema.function`, written in SQL or Python. Creating one needs `USAGE` and `CREATE` on the schema plus `USAGE` on the catalog. Running one needs `EXECUTE` on the function plus `USAGE` on the schema and catalog. Python code in these UDFs needs a serverless or pro SQL warehouse, or a cluster on a supported runtime; a view that includes a Unity Catalog Python UDF fails on a classic SQL warehouse even when every privilege is granted. So when a UDF works in a notebook and fails in a dashboard, compare the compute type before touching grants. By default, Python UDFs with the same owner and session can share an isolation environment, which saves memory. The `STRICT ISOLATION` characteristic guarantees that a UDF runs in its own isolated environment; add it to UDFs that run input as code with `exec()` or `eval()`, write local files, change global state or access environment variables.

concepts.heading: Evaluation Order and Null Handling
concepts.body: Spark SQL, including the DataFrame API, does not guarantee the order in which subexpressions are evaluated. Inputs of an operator are not necessarily evaluated left to right, and `AND` and `OR` have no guaranteed short-circuiting. The optimizer can reorder predicates in `WHERE` and `HAVING`, so a UDF may receive rows that an earlier condition such as `s IS NOT NULL` was meant to exclude. A query like `WHERE s IS NOT NULL AND strlen(s) > 1` can fail with a null error only after a plan change, which makes the bug intermittent and hard to trace. The supported defenses are to make the UDF null-aware itself, or to wrap the call so the guard is part of one expression, for example `CASE WHEN s IS NOT NULL THEN strlen(s) END`. Do not rely on filter placement, and do not assume that a passing test on one plan proves the order. The same rule applies to any side effect or exception in a UDF: validate inputs inside the function.

examPoints: Large or regular workloads should use built-in functions such as `regexp_extract`; a Python UDF is the choice for hard logic, ad hoc work and moderate data.

Repeated model loading per batch is fixed with an Iterator pandas UDF that initializes once; a UDF that works in a notebook but fails in a view on a dashboard points to a classic SQL warehouse, not to privileges.
Null errors that appear after a plan change come from unguaranteed evaluation order, fixed by null-aware UDFs or `CASE WHEN`; `STRICT ISOLATION` is for UDFs that run code or touch files and state.

quiz.q: A scalar `pd.Series -> pd.Series` UDF scores 800 million rows and loads a 600 MB model inside the function. Executors spend most time deserializing the model. Which design removes the repeated load?
choices: Increase the batch size so the same model is deserialized for fewer, larger rows
Convert the logic to a row-by-row Python UDF that caches the model in a global
An iterator pandas UDF that loads the model once before the loop
Add the `STRICT ISOLATION` characteristic so that each batch gets its own fresh isolated environment
quiz.explain: The iterator form receives all batches of a task in one call, so initialization before the loop happens once. A larger batch only reduces the count, a row-by-row UDF is slower, and strict isolation adds separate environments instead of sharing work.

quiz.q: A Unity Catalog Python UDF is used in a view. Dashboards on a classic SQL warehouse fail on the view, while a notebook cluster works. `EXECUTE` and `SELECT` are granted. What should the team do?
choices: Grant `USAGE` on every catalog in the workspace to the dashboard owner and viewers
Re-create the function as a built-in that skips the catalog and schema name
Run the dashboards on a serverless or pro SQL warehouse
Add `STRICT ISOLATION` to the function so the classic warehouse accepts it
quiz.explain: Views that contain Unity Catalog Python UDFs fail on classic SQL warehouses, so the compute type is the problem. Extra grants cannot fix it, built-ins cannot be re-created that way, and isolation only changes how the UDF runs.

recap: Prefer built-ins at scale, use iterator pandas UDFs to initialize once, remember that Unity Catalog Python UDFs depend on compute type and need EXECUTE, and never rely on predicate order to guard a UDF.

title: Lakeflow Pipelines with Auto Loader, and Structured Streaming versus Declarative Pipelines

concepts.heading: Auto Loader Discovery, Backfills and Restarts
concepts.body: The associate guide covers Auto Loader basics, so this day covers failure behavior. With `cloudFiles.useManagedFileEvents` set to `true`, the first run lists the whole load path to synchronize with the file events cache and stores a read position in the checkpoint. Later runs read new-file notifications and skip the listing. If a stream stays stopped for more than seven days, that read position expires and the next run does a full listing again: nothing is lost or duplicated, but the run is slow, so run such streams at least weekly. In directory listing and classic notification modes a file can still be missed, for example during a storage incident. A backfill is a periodic asynchronous directory listing that catches missed files, and it runs only if you set `cloudFiles.backfillInterval`, which has no default. With the default `addNewColumns` schema evolution mode and no explicit schema, a new source column stops the stream with `UnknownFieldException` on purpose; the restart succeeds with the new schema, so run it as a Lakeflow Jobs task with retries instead of paging an operator.

concepts.heading: Streaming Tables, Refreshes and Append Flows
concepts.body: A streaming table processes each input record once and expects an append-only source. If an upstream Delta table gets updates or deletes, such as a GDPR purge, the stream fails by default. `skipChangeCommits` processes only appended rows and ignores the other commits, which fits when the deletion is handled separately in each layer. Refresh semantics matter most for history. A default refresh uses the stored checkpoint. A full refresh clears the table data and the flow checkpoints and reprocesses everything the source still has, so records already removed by a storage lifecycle rule or a short Kafka retention are dropped from the target. Setting the table property `pipelines.reset.allowed` to `false` blocks full refreshes. Resetting only the checkpoints of selected flows, through the pipeline update API, restarts reading without clearing the table. To add sources, use multiple append flows into one streaming table, each with its own checkpoint, and a one-time `ONCE` flow for a historical backfill, with no full refresh and no `UNION`.

concepts.heading: Pipeline Mode and Who Controls It
concepts.body: Pipeline mode is independent of the dataset type. A triggered update processes the data available when it starts and stops, so compute costs exist only during the update; it fits freshness of ten minutes, hourly or daily. A continuous pipeline keeps running and fits freshness of seconds to a few minutes but needs always-on compute. When a job orchestrates a pipeline, the job decides: a triggered or scheduled job runs one update and stops even if the pipeline mode says continuous, and a continuous job runs the pipeline continuously even if the mode is triggered. Databricks recommends running continuous pipelines as a continuous job and leaving the pipeline mode on triggered. For twenty-five tables with a thirty-minute freshness target and lowest cost, one triggered pipeline started every thirty minutes beats always-on queries. On serverless compute for jobs, `Trigger.ProcessingTime` and `Trigger.Continuous` are rejected with `INFINITE_STREAMING_TRIGGER_NOT_SUPPORTED`; use `Trigger.AvailableNow` or move the logic into a continuous serverless pipeline.

concepts.heading: Structured Streaming or Declarative Pipelines
concepts.body: A pipeline is a set of declared datasets (streaming tables, materialized views, views) and flows. The engine analyzes dependencies before running, plans the order, retries flows and manages checkpoints. That static planning explains the restrictions. `pivot()` has to read the data to learn the pivot values, so a pipeline rejects it; rewrite it with conditional aggregation such as `SUM(CASE WHEN metric = 'cpu' THEN value END)`. Each dataset can be defined only once across pipelines, except for append flows on a streaming table, so two teams writing the same table need one definition plus one flow per topic. Time travel queries work on streaming tables but not on materialized views. Arbitrary side effects inside dataset functions are not a supported design. When each micro-batch must write a table, call a REST service and run a `MERGE` over JDBC in one function, use Structured Streaming with `foreachBatch` as a Lakeflow Jobs task. When the work is declarative transformation and CDC, prefer the pipeline.

examPoints: Know Auto Loader recovery: stopped more than seven days with file events means a full listing, `cloudFiles.backfillInterval` is opt-in, and the default schema mode fails once on purpose and needs a retry.
Full refresh drops history the source no longer has; `pipelines.reset.allowed` protects it, and append flows or checkpoint resets add or restart sources without clearing the table.
The job's mode overrides the pipeline's, `pivot()` and duplicate dataset definitions are pipeline limits, and custom per-batch side effects belong to `foreachBatch`.

quiz.q: A streaming table `bronze_events` holds two years of history from JSON files, and a lifecycle rule deletes the source files after 30 days. A full refresh left only the last month. Which setting would have prevented it?
choices: Setting `cloudFiles.backfillInterval` to one year so older files are re-listed
Set the table property `pipelines.reset.allowed` to `false`
Switching the whole pipeline to continuous mode so that the stream never needs any refresh again
Setting `skipChangeCommits` on the stream so deleted files are never reprocessed
quiz.explain: A full refresh clears the table and reprocesses only files that still exist, so the property that blocks full refreshes protects the history. A backfill lists existing files only, continuous mode does not stop a manual refresh, and skipChangeCommits concerns upstream Delta commits.

quiz.q: A pipeline's mode is continuous, but operations wrap it in a job with an hourly schedule. How does it behave, and what is recommended for continuous processing?
choices: It runs continuously and the hourly schedule is ignored, so no other job setting is needed at all
The job takes precedence, so each run is one update; use a continuous job
The pipeline fails to start because a scheduled job cannot start a pipeline in continuous mode
The pipeline mode takes precedence, so the job only monitors updates it never starts
quiz.explain: When a job orchestrates a pipeline it decides the execution mode, so an hourly job gives one update per run. Databricks recommends a continuous job for continuous processing. The other choices reverse precedence or invent a failure.

recap: Auto Loader recovers through retries, backfills and weekly runs; a full refresh can destroy history; the job beats the pipeline mode; and Structured Streaming with foreachBatch handles custom side effects that declarative pipelines do not.

title: Streaming Table or Materialized View, and AUTO CDC for SCD Types 1 and 2

concepts.heading: Choosing the Dataset Type
concepts.body: A streaming table processes each input record once and keeps what it has ingested even if the source later loses it. A materialized view guarantees that its result equals the batch query over the current inputs, recomputing incrementally or fully as needed. Choose by the requirement. Bronze ingestion of files that a lifecycle rule archives after thirty days needs a streaming table, because history must outlive the source. A report that must show the current customer segment for all historical orders needs a materialized view, because a stream-static join in a streaming table joins each row once, with the dimension as it was then, and later dimension changes never touch written rows. A low-latency windowed aggregation of append-only events over the clock needs a streaming table with a watermark in a continuous pipeline; a materialized view has refresh latency of seconds to minutes. Changing a streaming table's query affects only new rows. To reprocess history, run a full refresh of only that table when its source still holds the complete history.

concepts.heading: Materialized View Refresh Behavior
concepts.body: A materialized view refreshes incrementally only on serverless pipelines; classic pipelines always recompute fully. Even on serverless, incremental refresh is cost-based and best effort: the engine may pick a full recompute, though the result is identical. Summing `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE` values gives order-dependent results, so the engine cannot update a previous aggregate incrementally and plans a full refresh. Casting the value to a decimal type makes incremental planning possible. Some incremental operations also need row tracking on the source tables, and a source recreated without it can silently push the view back to full recompute. The planning information in the pipeline event log shows why a refresh was full. A refresh policy makes the intent explicit. `AUTO` is cost-based, `INCREMENTAL` prefers incremental but may fall back, and `INCREMENTAL STRICT` requires incremental refresh and fails if that is not possible. Use the strict policy when an unexpected full refresh would break the SLA or budget and you would rather debug a failure.

concepts.heading: AUTO CDC Mechanics for SCD Type 1 and Type 2
concepts.body: `AUTO CDC` (formerly APPLY CHANGES) applies change events in the order of `sequence_by`, not arrival order. The column must be sortable, follow the true order of changes in the source, and be non-null; a log position or commit version works, while `current_timestamp()` added in the pipeline records processing time and lets old values overwrite newer ones. Delete events need a real sequence value too. In Type 1 the target keeps the latest values; an older event arriving late is ignored. In Type 2 the target stores versions with `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`: a change closes the current version and opens a new one, a delete closes the current version with the delete's sequence value, and active rows have `__END_AT IS NULL`. `track_history_except_column_list` stops a noisy column such as `last_seen_at` from creating new versions. For partial updates that send NULL for unchanged columns, `ignore_null_updates_column_list` protects only the listed columns, so NULL can still clear the others.

concepts.heading: Snapshots and Downstream Reads of CDC Targets
concepts.body: When a source offers no change log, only periodic full extracts, `AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT` compares consecutive snapshots, derives inserts, updates and deletes, and applies Type 1 or Type 2 logic. Snapshots must be processed in increasing version order, so a non-increasing version fails the update. Products absent from a newer snapshot are closed in Type 2, and two price changes between snapshots appear as one change because only the two states are visible. The target of an AUTO CDC flow is updated and deleted in place, so it is not an append-only source. A plain streaming read of it fails on commits that update or delete files, and `skipChangeCommits` would silently drop the changes, making a downstream count wrong. The correct downstream dataset is a materialized view over the target, which recomputes, incrementally where supported, whenever the target changes. For comparison, a hand-written `MERGE` in `foreachBatch` must handle duplicates in a batch, late events and deletes by itself; AUTO CDC removes that code.

examPoints: Streaming table for history and per-row-once logic, materialized view for results that must match current inputs; do not enrich with a mutable dimension inside a streaming table when history must reflect new values.
Incremental materialized view refresh needs serverless, decimal instead of DOUBLE sums and row tracking where required; `INCREMENTAL STRICT` makes a silent full refresh fail loudly.
AUTO CDC needs a non-null `sequence_by` that follows source order, Type 2 closes versions with `__END_AT`, and a downstream aggregate of a CDC target is a materialized view.

quiz.q: An AUTO CDC flow applies a Debezium topic with `sequence_by = F.current_timestamp()` added upstream. Messages from different partitions arrive out of order and old values sometimes replace newer ones. What is the root cause and fix?
choices: Sequence follows processing time; use a source commit position as `sequence_by`
The flow is set to Type 1, so switch to Type 2 and every late event is kept in order
The pipeline is in triggered mode, so switch to continuous and arrival order becomes reliable
The key columns are missing, so add all columns as keys to let the flow sort the events
quiz.explain: AUTO CDC compares sequence values, and processing time does not reflect the order of changes in the source. Switching Type or mode does not repair a wrong ordering column, and adding keys changes row identity, not ordering.

quiz.q: A silver table is an AUTO CDC Type 1 target with upserts and deletes. A gold dataset must always match the active-customer count per region. Which definition is correct?
choices: A streaming table that reads silver with `skipChangeCommits` and counts the appended rows only
A materialized view that aggregates silver and is recomputed when silver changes
A streaming table that reads silver with `delta.appendOnly` enabled on the source
A streaming table with a watermark on the silver update time and an append output
quiz.explain: The CDC target is changed in place, so downstream aggregates must be recomputed from its current state. Ignoring change commits loses updates and deletes, and an append-only property forbids the updates and deletes that the target needs.

recap: Streaming tables keep history, materialized views track current inputs, refresh policies control incremental behavior, and AUTO CDC depends on a correct non-null sequence column.

title: Lakeflow Jobs: UI, API and CLI, Control Flow, and Compute Choices

concepts.heading: Creating, Changing and Starting Jobs Programmatically
concepts.body: The Databricks CLI wraps the Jobs REST API, so each command maps to a request. The classic trap is `reset` versus `update`. `jobs reset` overwrites all settings of the job with the supplied definition, so a file containing only a `schedule` removes the tasks and cluster settings and the next run fails. `jobs update` adds, changes or removes specific settings and leaves the rest. Starting a run has three paths. A schedule or trigger starts it from the definition, `run-now` starts an existing job, and `submit` takes a definition and triggers a one-time run: the job is not saved, does not appear in the Jobs UI, and does not retry on failure. Because it is not saved, serverless compute cannot be auto-optimized after failures, so explicit classic settings may suit a one-off integration check. For an external scheduler that retries on timeouts, `run-now` accepts an `idempotency_token` of up to 64 characters; reusing the token returns the existing run, so exactly one run is launched.

concepts.heading: Parameters Reach Tasks in Two Styles
concepts.body: Tasks take parameters in two forms. Key-value tasks (notebook, SQL, Run Job, and Python wheel keyword arguments) receive job parameters automatically, and if a task parameter has the same key as a job parameter, the job parameter wins. Tasks that take a JSON array of strings (Python script, Python wheel positional arguments, JAR, Spark Submit and For each) receive only what the array contains, as if run from a command line. A Python script that expects `run_date` must therefore have `{{job.parameters.run_date}}` written into its array. Task values pass small scalar results between tasks, such as a count or a path, and a task reads them with `{{tasks.<name>.values.<key>}}`. An If/else condition task compares two operands: `==` and `!=` compare as strings, while `>`, `>=`, `<` and `<=` compare numerically. Only numeric, string and boolean task values are allowed, so a Python list makes the condition fail; set a scalar such as a bad-record count and compare it with `> 0`.

concepts.heading: Run If, For Each and Repair
concepts.body: The Run if setting decides whether a task runs given the outcome of its dependencies. A task whose Run if condition is not met is Excluded, for example with At least one failed. An Excluded upstream task counts as successful for dependants, and if all dependencies of a task are Excluded the task is Excluded too, whatever its own Run if says, cascading down a chain. To have a final report run every night, make it depend on the main task as well and set Run if to All done. A For each task runs a nested task once per element of an input array. Concurrency defaults to 1, so 150 four-minute iterations take ten hours until you raise it, a capacity decision for compute and sources. The nested task cannot be another For each task; flatten a cross product into one array of objects read as `{{input.region}}`. For long lists, build the array in an upstream task and reference its task value. Repair re-runs only unsuccessful tasks and their dependants, and works only for jobs with two or more tasks.

concepts.heading: Compute and Environment Choices for Tasks
concepts.body: Databricks recommends serverless compute for most automated workloads: fewer settings, fast start-up and automatic scaling. Classic jobs compute is for non-SQL tasks that need what serverless does not offer, such as compute-scoped init scripts that install an operating system package, or compute policies. Serverless installs Python packages through the environment, a base environment plus a dependency list. It also rejects some APIs: `df.checkpoint()`, `spark.catalog.cacheTable()` and `CACHE TABLE` raise exceptions, while `df.cache()` and `df.persist()` work; replace a checkpoint with a write to a Delta table. Global temporary views are not supported, so tasks that exchange data should share a table, since each task runs in an isolated environment. For streaming, only triggers that end on their own run on serverless jobs, so an always-on query with a short processing interval belongs in a continuous serverless pipeline. A heavy classic pipeline that hits out-of-memory on skewed batches can move to serverless, which adds vertical autoscaling on top of horizontal.

examPoints: `jobs reset` overwrites the whole definition and `jobs update` patches; `run-now` with an `idempotency_token` prevents duplicate runs, and `submit` is an unsaved one-time run without retries.
Python script tasks need job parameters written into the JSON array, If/else accepts only scalar task values, and Excluded tasks cascade through Run if conditions.
Serverless is the default, classic compute is for init scripts and custom settings, and serverless limits include triggers, `checkpoint()`, `cacheTable()` and global temporary views.

quiz.q: A CI step updates a job from a JSON file that contains only the new `schedule` block using `databricks jobs reset`. Afterward the job has no tasks. What is the right approach for partial changes?
choices: Use `databricks jobs submit` so the schedule is added without touching the saved job
Reset overwrites all settings, so partial changes use `databricks jobs update`
Add `max_concurrent_runs` to the file so reset keeps the existing task settings
Use `run-now` with an `idempotency_token` so that the saved job gets the new schedule applied
quiz.explain: `reset` replaces everything missing from the file, while `update` changes only the specified settings. `submit` creates an unsaved one-time run, concurrency settings do not preserve tasks, and `run-now` starts runs rather than editing the job.

quiz.q: A job has `process`, then `cleanup` (Run if At least one failed), then `report` depending only on `cleanup`. On successful nights `report` does not run. What is the right change?
choices: Set Run if All succeeded on `cleanup` so the report follows it every night
Make `report` depend on `process` too, with Run if All done
Enable repair on the job so skipped tasks are re-run when the night ends
Move `report` into a For each task with concurrency greater than 1 over the main task
quiz.explain: When every dependency of a task is Excluded, the task is Excluded regardless of its own Run if. Depending on `process` as well, with All done, makes the report run whatever happens. Repair is for failed runs and For each does not change dependency evaluation.

recap: Know reset versus update, the three ways to start a run, idempotency tokens, how parameters reach each task type, how Excluded cascades, and which serverless limits push work to classic compute or a pipeline.

title: Testing Pipeline Code and Stateful Structured Streaming

concepts.heading: Testable Pipeline Code
concepts.body: Databricks recommends keeping Python functions and their tests outside notebooks: import functions from a module in a Git folder or a bundle source folder and test them with `pytest`. Separate logic from I/O. A transformation is a pure function from DataFrame to DataFrame, covered by unit tests with a handful of in-memory rows, while a thin entry point reads and writes the real tables. Tests should use fake data, never production tables, particularly for code that changes data. Two ways to run Spark exist in tests. Local PySpark gives fast unit tests on a laptop or CI runner with no workspace. Databricks Connect runs code on remote compute through Spark Connect and suits integration tests that must read Unity Catalog tables or run on the real runtime. The two conflict: `databricks-connect` ships its own `pyspark` module, so an image built with both fails with Spark session errors. Uninstall the standalone PySpark in the Connect environment and run local unit tests in a separate environment.

concepts.heading: Comparing DataFrames Correctly
concepts.body: A test such as `actual.collect() == expected.collect()` is brittle. Spark gives no ordering guarantee after a shuffle, and floating-point aggregates can differ in the last digits when values are added in a different order. `assertDataFrameEqual` from `pyspark.testing` compares schema and rows, ignores row order by default, and compares numeric values with a relative and absolute tolerance. Schema is part of equality. Column types must match unless `ignoreColumnType=True`, nullability is ignored by default, and column order matters unless `ignoreColumnOrder=True`. A common trap: `createDataFrame` from Python tuples infers integers as `LongType`, while a function that casts to `int` returns `IntegerType`. Values print identically and the assertion fails. Declare an explicit schema for the expected DataFrame instead of loosening the check, so the test also guards the output contract.

concepts.heading: Watermarks, Output Modes and State
concepts.body: A watermark is the maximum event time seen minus the threshold, set at the start of each trigger. Data less than the threshold behind the latest data is guaranteed to be aggregated; data later than that is not guaranteed to be dropped, so the guarantee is strict in one direction only. Append mode writes a window once, after the watermark passes its end, so every result is delayed by the threshold. Update mode writes changed rows as soon as they change, so a dashboard sees partial totals early, and state is still dropped after the watermark. Complete mode rewrites the whole result and never drops aggregation state. With several watermarked inputs the global watermark defaults to the `min` policy, the slowest stream, which keeps late data but holds state longer; `multipleWatermarkPolicy` set to `max` follows the fastest and risks dropping the slower feed's records. Stream-stream joins support append mode only. Outer joins need watermarks on both inputs plus an event-time range condition, and unmatched rows are emitted with NULLs after the watermark passes.

concepts.heading: foreachBatch, Checkpoints and Recovery
concepts.body: `foreachBatch` gives at-least-once guarantees. The checkpoint's offset log records a planned batch before it runs and the commit log records it afterwards, so a failure between two writes replays the same batch with the same `batchId`. For Delta writes, set `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` bound to `batchId` so a replayed write is skipped, and let errors propagate so the job retries the whole batch. A batch that has an offset entry but no commit is re-planned with exactly the same offsets. Lowering `maxFilesPerTrigger` after an out-of-memory failure therefore applies only to later batches; the first replayed batch needs more compute. With a stateful operator such as `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`, the function must consume the whole batch DataFrame, even on a skip path. Reading part of it with `limit`, `show(2)` or an early `return` leaves state inconsistent and the next batch fails.

examPoints: Unit tests use local PySpark and pure DataFrame functions; integration tests use Databricks Connect, and the two packages conflict in one environment.
Use `assertDataFrameEqual` with an explicit expected schema, and remember the watermark guarantee is one-directional; update mode lowers latency, append mode waits for the watermark.
foreachBatch is at-least-once: use `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` for idempotence, expect replays to reuse old offsets, and always consume the whole batch with stateful operators.

quiz.q: A unit test builds the expected DataFrame with `createDataFrame([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')], ['id', 'code'])`. The function under test returns `id` cast to `int`. The values look identical but `assertDataFrameEqual` fails. What is the cause and the fix?
choices: Row order differs after the shuffle, so set `checkRowOrder=True` on the comparison
Nullability differs, so set `ignoreNullable=False` to let the check pass for both frames
Inferred `LongType` differs from `IntegerType`; declare the expected schema
The tolerance is too tight, so raise `rtol` until the integer columns compare equal
quiz.explain: Schema is part of equality, and inferred Python integers are 64-bit while a cast to `int` is 32-bit. An explicit expected schema fixes the test honestly. Row order is ignored by default, nullability is ignored by default, and tolerances do not apply to type mismatches.

quiz.q: A `foreachBatch` function appends each micro-batch to `silver.orders` then to `silver.orders_audit`. After a failure between the writes and a job retry, `silver.orders` holds the batch twice. Which change gives the strongest guarantee?
choices: Write both tables with `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` bound to `batchId`
Wrap each write in a `try/except` that swallows the error so that the checkpoint commits the whole batch
Lower `maxFilesPerTrigger` so each batch contains too few rows to be written twice
Switch the stream to complete output mode so every batch overwrites the earlier rows
quiz.explain: A replayed batch keeps its `batchId`, so idempotent Delta writes skip data that was already committed. Swallowing errors commits a half-written batch, the trigger limit does not stop replays, and output mode does not govern a custom foreachBatch sink.

recap: Test pure functions with pytest and explicit schemas, keep Connect and PySpark apart, choose output modes by latency versus completeness, and make foreachBatch writes idempotent with txnAppId and txnVersion.
